Nob
NOB
proper noun
Hebrew Nob, perhaps “high place,” a town of the priests near Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood for a time.

See also: Nob

📖 Biblical Definition

Nob was a town of the priests, lying a little north of Jerusalem, where the tabernacle and the priestly house of Ahimelech served in the days of Saul. Thither David fled when he escaped from the court, and Ahimelech the priest, though afraid at his coming, gave him the hallowed shewbread and the sword of Goliath (1Sa 21:1). The Lord Jesus afterward used that very act to teach mercy above ritual, recalling how David entered the house of God and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful but for the priests (Mat 12:4). But Nob is remembered most for the dreadful vengeance of Saul. When Doeg the Edomite reported what Ahimelech had done, the jealous king commanded the priests slain, and Nob, the city of the priests, he smote with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep (1Sa 22:19). The dictionary marks Nob as the city of priestly blood, where a king mad with envy turned his sword upon the ministers of God. Centuries later Isaiah set the Assyrian invader at Nob, shaking his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion (Isa 10:32). The town stands as a witness against the persecution of God’s servants, and a pledge that the blood of His priests is precious in His sight.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A city of the priests near Jerusalem, massacred by Saul after Ahimelech aided David.

expand to see more

NOB, a town of the priests lying north of Jerusalem.

There the tabernacle and the house of Ahimelech served in Saul’s day.

Ahimelech gave David the hallowed shewbread and the sword of Goliath.

Saul, enraged by Doeg’s report, smote the city of the priests with the sword.

It is the city of priestly blood, a witness against the persecution of God’s servants.

📖 Key Scripture

1Sa 21:1 — "Then came David to Nob to Ahimelech the priest: and Ahimelech was afraid at the meeting of David, and said unto him, Why art thou alone, and no man with thee?"

1Sa 22:19 — "And Nob, the city of the priests, smote he with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep, with the edge of the sword."

Mat 12:4 — "How he entered into the house of God, and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for them which were with him, but only for the priests?"

Isa 10:32 — "As yet shall he remain at Nob that day: he shall shake his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it stands as a witness against the persecution of God’s ministers.

expand to see more

Nob has met no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the scene of one of the bloodiest crimes of Saul’s reign. The dictionary records the town that the reader may know what the envy of a forsaken king did to the priests of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the preciousness of the blood of God’s servants and the certain judgment upon their persecutors. Saul, mad with jealousy, smote the city of the priests; Doeg the Edomite did the deed his master commanded. But the blood of the saints is not forgotten in heaven, and the persecutor who lifts his hand against the ministers of God shakes it in vain against the mount of Zion, whose Lord avenges His own.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew perhaps “high place,” Nob names the city of the priests Saul put to the sword.

Usage

"Like Nob under Saul’s sword, the persecution of God’s ministers cries to heaven for justice."

"The Lord taught from Ahimelech’s shewbread that mercy stands above mere ritual."

"The blood of the saints is precious in His sight, and their persecutors shake their hand in vain."
